idiom_name: bounded attempt loop with classified failures and an interruptible delay
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: wrap the operation in a loop that (1) invokes it, (2) on failure asks a predicate whether this error is transient, (3) if the attempt budget or deadline is not exhausted waits for the policy's delay and tries again, (4) otherwise rethrows or returns the last failure. Keep three things separate - the operation, the classification predicate and the delay schedule - so the same loop serves every dependency and only the policy differs. Bound it twice: a maximum number of attempts and a maximum total time measured across attempts and delays. Make the wait interruptible (cancellation token, context, signal) and log each attempt at a lower level than the exhausted failure.
pitfalls: A loop with no attempt cap and no deadline never terminates when the failure turns out to be permanent.
Retrying every exception - including programming errors and validation failures - hides bugs and multiplies load.
Sharing one attempt counter across concurrent calls corrupts the policy; the state belongs to the call.
Sleeping without cancellation support delays shutdown and ignores the caller's deadline.
A loop with no attempt cap and no deadline never terminates when the failure turns out to be permanent.
Retrying every exception — including programming errors and validation failures — hides bugs and multiplies load on the failing service.
Sharing one attempt counter across concurrent calls corrupts the policy; the state belongs to the individual call.
Sleeping without cancellation support delays shutdown and ignores the caller's deadline.
Pure exponential backoff without jitter causes a thundering herd: all concurrent clients retry at identical intervals, spiking the dependency's load exactly when it is recovering.
Ignoring the Retry-After header when retrying HTTP 503 or 429 wastes the server's recovery window and may push retries into an ongoing throttle window.
Stacking retry policies at multiple layers (SDK + client + handler + broker) multiplies attempts: one logical failure can become dozens of redundant calls.

A retry policy that does not bound total elapsed time will wait out the entire retry schedule even when the caller's HTTP request has already timed out, wasting resources on work nobody is waiting for.

Retrying on HTTP 404 is safe only for eventually-consistent reads; retrying a missing DELETE or a missing idempotent PUT is harmless, but retrying a missing GET that returned a 404 is at best useless and at worst confusing in logs.
Logging every retry attempt as ERROR causes alert fatigue; use INFO/DEBUG for individual attempts and only ERROR (or a dedicated retry_exhausted metric) for the final failure.

In deep fan-out call graphs, each layer retrying independently multiplies load at the deepest layer by the product of all layers' retry counts; this can turn a single failed dependency into a stack-wide retry storm.

A retry budget that is shared across concurrent calls without per-call accounting allows one caller to consume the entire budget, starving other concurrent calls that have legitimate transient failures.

Using a fixed seed for the random number generator that produces jitter values causes all clients started with the same seed to generate identical jitter sequences, recreating the thundering herd problem even with jitter configured.

Wrong move: assume max_attempts always means retries rather than total attempts -> the effective budget can exceed the intended limit -> instead verify the SDK's counting semantics and derive the deadline from total attempts.
